title: Getting Sponsored at 16 Almost Ruined Skating for Me
creator: Nico Ferreira
description:
Storytime. I got my first shoe sponsor at sixteen, lost it at nineteen, and it took me years to actually enjoy skating again.

Filmed at the old Eastside plaza, which is getting torn down next spring.

Clips from 2011 to 2014 filmed by my brother Rafa on a Canon camcorder that still works somehow.

Thanks for all the questions on the last video.

sentences.t: So a lot of you asked in the comments on the last video how I got sponsored, and why I stopped skating for like four years.
And those are kind of the same story, so I figured I'd just sit down and tell it.
I'm at the old plaza where I basically grew up, it's getting torn down next spring, so it felt right.
Okay, so I started skating at eleven, on a board my cousin left at our house.
I was terrible, like, genuinely terrible, it took me a whole summer to learn an ollie.
But I was here every day, after school, weekends, I'd stay until the lights went off.
And by fifteen I was decent, and my brother started filming me with this old camcorder.
We'd put the clips online, and a few of them did okay, like a few thousand views, which back then felt huge.
Then, when I was sixteen, I got an email from the team manager at Halcyon Shoes.
They wanted to sponsor me, which for a sixteen year old skater is basically the dream, it's the thing you think about every night.
At first it was just flow, so free shoes every couple of months, and then a year later they put me on the actual team with a small monthly check.
I remember calling my mom from the parking lot screaming, she thought something terrible had happened.
And for a while it was the best thing ever, I got to go on a tour, I met skaters I'd been watching for years.
But here's the part people don't really talk about.
Once someone's paying you, skating isn't really yours anymore.
Every session I'd be thinking, is this footage good enough, am I landing enough new tricks, are they going to drop me.
I stopped skating for fun completely, I stopped coming here just to hang out, every session was a shoot.
And I got hurt, I broke my wrist at eighteen trying a rail I definitely wasn't ready for.
I tried it because there was a filmer there and I felt like I had to deliver.
I was off the board for five months, and when I came back, I wasn't as good, and I was scared.
And at nineteen I got the call, they were restructuring the team, and I was off.
Honestly, they were really nice about it, nobody did anything wrong, that's just how it works.
But I was so burned out that I just put the board in my closet and didn't touch it for four years.
I went to college, I got a normal job, and I kind of told myself that part of my life was over.
And then, about two years ago, my nephew asked me to teach him to skate.
So I took him to this exact spot, and I was just helping him roll, holding his hands, and I felt that thing again.
No camera, no pressure, just rolling around because it's fun.
And now I'm here basically every weekend, I'm worse than I was at seventeen, and I'm having way more fun.
So if you're young and you're grinding for that first sponsor, I'm not saying don't go for it.
Just, make sure you still have sessions where nobody's filming and nothing's at stake.
Okay, I'm going to go skate the ledge one more time before they tear it down.
Thanks for listening to me ramble, see you.
